name: Lingual braces

angle.text: Users choose lingual braces to straighten teeth without visible brackets on the front surfaces, so the smile improves while treatment is under way. Alignment by braces is well studied; forum posters also discuss face-shape changes with extractions, which is based on anecdote.

summary: Braces bonded behind the teeth to hide them; discreet, but linked to more tongue and speech trouble than outer braces.
note: Evidence concerns tooth alignment, not facial structure; reviews report more tongue pain and speech difficulty.
currentQuick:
Lingual braces are fixed braces attached to the tongue side of the teeth, so they are hard to see. They were first developed in California in the mid-1970s.
They are used to straighten teeth and correct bites. Forum discussion is mostly about braces in general and whether they change facial structure, a question with little direct research.
How it works: Brackets and wires on the inner tooth surfaces apply steady forces that move teeth, the same principle as braces on the outer surfaces.
Risks and caveats: A 2016 review summarised in encyclopedic sources reports more tongue pain, speech and eating difficulty and harder cleaning than with outer braces; brackets break more often in some designs. White spot lesions can still occur with poor hygiene. Treatment is delivered by orthodontists.
deepLead:
Lingual braces are fixed orthodontic appliances bonded to the tongue-facing (inner) surfaces of the teeth rather than the outer surfaces, so that they are largely hidden from view. 
They are used for the same purposes as conventional braces, such as straightening teeth and correcting bite problems. Encyclopedic accounts and a 2016 systematic review summarised there report that lingual appliances are associated with more tongue pain, harder oral hygiene and more speech and eating difficulty than labial braces, and that mechanical finishing is harder because the brackets sit closer together. 
In looksmaxxing communities, braces in general are discussed mainly in terms of whether they improve the smile or can alter facial structure; lingual braces as a separate topic appear far less often than discussion of braces overall.

name: Miswak / chew stick

angle.text: Miswak is used as a traditional natural toothbrush, and some people also use it hoping for cleaner, whiter-looking teeth. Small trials have looked at plaque reduction; whitening specifically is untested.

summary: A traditional twig toothbrush from the arak tree; small trials link it to less plaque, but whitening claims are untested.
note: Trials measure plaque and gum health, not tooth colour; study quality is mixed.
currentQuick:
Miswak is a chewing stick cut from the Salvadora persica tree, used for centuries in the Middle East, Africa and South Asia and valued in Islamic tradition. The frayed end works as a natural brush.
Reviews report reductions in plaque and gum inflammation in small trials, and it is also used for fresher breath and in traditional accounts for whiter teeth. No controlled trial of whitening was found.
How it works: The fibres scrub plaque from the teeth, and plant compounds such as benzyl isothiocyanate have shown antibacterial activity in laboratory tests. A trial also reported higher plaque pH after rinsing with the extract.
Risks and caveats: Reviews describe it as low-risk and cheap, but they also note variable study quality and the need for larger trials. Comparisons cited on Wikipedia show lower antibacterial activity than chlorhexidine. A dental-journal letter discusses misuse of the stick.
deepLead:
Miswak is a traditional tooth-cleaning stick made from the twigs, stems or roots of the Salvadora persica tree, also called the arak or peelu tree. One end is chewed or peeled to expose fibres that act as bristles. Neem twigs (Azadirachta indica) serve a similar purpose in parts of South Asia, where they are known as datun. 
The stick has been used for centuries across the Middle East, Africa and South Asia, and it holds religious significance in Islamic tradition.  People use it for oral hygiene, fresher breath and, in some accounts, a whiter and polished look to the teeth. 
Reviews of the clinical literature report that miswak use, alone or beside a toothbrush, is associated with reductions in plaque and gingival inflammation, though the trials are small and varied in design. Evidence that it whitens teeth is thinner and comes largely from descriptive accounts.

name: Colored / circle contact lenses

chain: Tinted or ringed lens over iris
Eye colour or iris size changes
angle.text: Users wear colored lenses to change eye colour, and circle lenses to make the iris look larger, an effect that is visible as soon as they are worn. Forum posters debate how much it adds to overall attractiveness, which is based on opinion rather than studies.

summary: Tinted or enlarging contact lenses that change eye colour; FDA treats them as prescription medical devices with infection risks.
note: FDA warns that unfitted or non-prescribed lenses can cause infection and vision loss.
currentQuick:
Coloured and circle lenses are cosmetic contacts that change the look of the iris, either by tinting it or by adding a ring that makes the eye appear larger. In forums they are mostly used to lighten dark eyes.
No studies were found that measure whether they raise perceived attractiveness, so the appearance benefit rests on user reports.
How it works: A printed pigment layer on the lens covers or modifies the iris colour, and circle lenses add a darker or larger outer rim to enlarge the visible iris.
Risks and caveats: The FDA classes decorative lenses as medical devices needing a prescription and lists corneal abrasion, allergy, reduced vision and infection that can lead to blindness. A case report notes that some circle lenses contain metals that can matter during MRI.
deepLead:
Colored contact lenses, also called cosmetic, decorative or fashion lenses, change the apparent colour of the eye. Circle lenses, also called big-eye lenses, are a type of cosmetic lens that adds a coloured or dark ring to enlarge the apparent size of the iris. 
In the United States the Food and Drug Administration regulates decorative lenses as medical devices, requires a prescription for them, and warns that lenses obtained without a proper fitting can cause corneal abrasion, allergic reactions, reduced vision and infections that may lead to blindness.
In looksmaxxing communities, coloured lenses are discussed as a way to lighten or contrast the eye colour, especially for people with dark brown eyes, and users debate shades, wear time and whether the result looks natural. No controlled study of their effect on perceived attractiveness was found.

name: Foot orthotic insoles

angle.text: Some insoles are sold for added height, which is measurable while worn, and others for comfort, gait or arch support that people hope will improve posture and standing presence. Trials cover heel pain; posture and looks effects are untested.

summary: Shoe inserts sold for comfort, gait and height; evidence is for heel pain, with none found for looks or posture.
note: Medical evidence is mixed and none was found for appearance, posture or height use in healthy people.
currentQuick:
Orthotic insoles are removable supports for the shoe, either custom made from a foot scan or bought ready made. They are sold for comfort, arch support, pain relief and, in some products, extra height.
Their best-studied use is heel pain from plantar fasciitis. No studies were found of them for posture, gait appearance or height in people without a foot problem.
How it works: They redistribute load across the foot and may hold the arch or heel in a set position; heel inserts also raise the heel by a small amount.
Risks and caveats: Reviews describe mixed evidence for medical use and inconsistent fit across methods. Documented harms of insoles themselves were not identified in the sources reviewed, but clinicians treat the underlying conditions with several measures, not insoles alone.
deepLead:
Foot orthotic insoles, also called shoe inserts, foot orthoses or orthotics, are removable supports placed inside footwear. They are sold for comfort, arch support, pain relief, orthopaedic correction, athletic performance and, in some products, added height. 
They are either custom made from a cast or scan of the foot or bought ready made. Medical uses are the best studied, notably heel pain from plantar fasciitis, where reviews list orthotics among first-line conservative measures.  Evidence for medical use is described as mixed, and no studies were found of insoles as a posture, gait-appearance or height tool in people without a foot condition.

name: Gynecomastia compression vest

angle.text: Men wear compression vests to flatten the chest so that gynecomastia is less visible under shirts, with the change showing immediately. The vest conceals rather than treats the tissue, and no studies test it.

summary: A tight vest that hides male chest tissue under clothes; it conceals gynecomastia but no studies test it.
note: Concealment only; persistent or painful breast enlargement is a medical question.
currentQuick:
A gynecomastia compression vest is an elastic undershirt that flattens the chest so enlarged male breast tissue shows less through clothing. It does not change the tissue underneath.
Gynecomastia is common in adolescence, and most teenage cases resolve within about two years. No studies were found that test compression garments for it.
How it works: Pressure from the elastic fabric holds the chest tissue flatter against the body, which changes the outline under a shirt.
Risks and caveats: No published safety data for these vests were found. Medical sources describe observation, medication and surgery as the management routes for persistent gynecomastia, and note that some causes, such as drugs or illness, are evaluated by clinicians.
deepLead:
A gynecomastia compression vest is a tight-fitting undershirt or vest, sold mainly to men, that presses the chest flat so that enlarged male breast tissue is less visible under clothing. It conceals rather than treats the condition. Gynecomastia is the benign enlargement of one or both male breasts caused by an imbalance between estrogens and androgens. 
No published studies were found that test compression garments for gynecomastia. Medical sources describe observation, medication and surgery as the management routes, and the Wikipedia article on the condition does not mention compression garments.

name: Spray-tan booth

angle.text: Users book spray-tan booths for an even, bronzed colour without UV exposure, visible within hours and fading over about a week. The colour change is well established; inhalation of the mist has not been studied in humans.

summary: Automated booth that mists DHA for a UV-free tan; the colour is reliable, but inhalation safety is unstudied in humans.
note: FDA approves DHA for external use only, not inhalation; cell and mouse studies report harm at tested doses.
currentQuick:
A spray-tan booth coats the body in a mist of dihydroxyacetone (DHA), which turns the outer skin layer brown without UV light. The colour fades over about 5 to 10 days.
The tanning effect itself is well described. What has not been tested in people is the effect of breathing the mist.
How it works: DHA reacts with amino acids in dead surface skin cells in a Maillard-type browning reaction. The colour fades as those cells shed.
Risks and caveats: The FDA has approved DHA for external use only, not for the eyes, lips, mucous membranes or inhalation, and booth spraying can make that exposure difficult to avoid. Cell and mouse studies report DNA damage, cell stress and lung inflammation; no human trials of booth inhalation were found. Contact dermatitis has been reported.
deepLead:
A spray-tan booth is an enclosed, automated cabin in which a fine mist of a sunless tanning solution is sprayed over the body. The active ingredient is dihydroxyacetone (DHA), a colourless sugar that reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin to produce a temporary brown colour. Professionals can also apply the solution by hand with an airbrush. 
The colour fades over roughly 3 to 10 days as the outer skin sheds, and it does not involve ultraviolet exposure, which is why sunless tanning is often presented as an alternative to sunbeds.  The US Food and Drug Administration has approved DHA for external use but not for use around the eyes or lips, on mucous membranes, or by inhalation, and Wikipedia notes that all-over booth spraying can make that exposure hard to avoid. 
Laboratory and animal studies have reported cell damage and lung effects after DHA exposure. No human trials of booth-related inhalation outcomes were found.

name: Bronzer

angle.text: Bronzer gives an instant tanned look for the day and washes off, and people use it on the face to match a body tan or add warmth. The tint is visible as soon as it is applied.

summary: A wash-off skin tint that gives an instant tanned look with no UV and no staying power.
note: Surface colour only: it rubs off, can streak or look orange, and gives no real sun protection.
currentQuick:
A bronzer is a cosmetic colorant, sold as a powder, lotion, gel, mousse or spray, that tints the skin until it is washed off. People use it for an instant tan look, to even out skin tone, or to add shading to the face and body.
It appears in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding circles as a quick cosmetic fix, and in bodybuilding as the colour layer used alongside spray tans on stage. It is different from a DHA self-tanner, which reacts with the skin to produce a longer-lasting colour.
How it works: Bronzers deposit colour on the outer surface of the skin. Common colourants described in encyclopedic sources include walnut extract, jojoba extract and caramel. Because the colour sits on top of the skin, it comes off with soap and water and can transfer to clothing.
Risks and caveats: Reported downsides are an orange or patchy look if applied unevenly, transfer onto clothing, and skin reactions in people allergic to ingredients such as fragrances or benzyl alcohol. A bronzer does not tan the skin and is not a sunscreen, and dermatology sources note that sunless products give no meaningful UV protection.
deepLead:
A bronzer is a cosmetic product that temporarily tints the skin to look tanned. It comes as powders, lotions, gels, mousses, sprays and tinted moisturizers, and the colour lasts until it is washed off with soap and water. It is often worn for a one-day tan or alongside a longer-lasting self-tanner.
Unlike dihydroxyacetone (DHA) self-tanners, which react chemically with the outermost skin layer, a bronzer only coats the surface. Common colourants include walnut oil extract, jojoba extract and caramel, and the product can rub off on clothing or look orange or splotchy if applied unevenly. Some formulations contain potential allergens such as benzyl alcohol, tocopherol and fragrance.
In looksmaxxing and fitness forums, bronzer is discussed as a quick way to add colour or facial shading, and in competitive bodybuilding it is part of stage tanning routines. No clinical studies of bronzer as an appearance product have been published.

name: Gradual tanning lotion

angle.text: Gradual tanning lotions are used to build a natural-looking tan over several days, with a slight colour change usually visible after the first application. The colour deepens with repeated use and is a visible, measurable change.

summary: A daily moisturizer with a mild self-tanning agent that builds a streak-resistant colour over several days.
note: Colour is cosmetic and fades within days; it does not protect against UV.
currentQuick:
A gradual tanning lotion is a moisturizer or body lotion that contains a small amount of a self-tanning agent, usually dihydroxyacetone (DHA). Applied regularly, it deepens skin colour step by step rather than in one dark application.
Proponents like it because slow build-up is less likely to leave streaks or an orange cast than a one-off self-tan. It is not a sunscreen and has not been tested in published appearance trials.
How it works: DHA is a simple sugar that reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin in a Maillard (browning) reaction. The brown pigments produced are not melanin and form without UV light. They fade over several days as the outer skin sheds, which is why gradual products are reapplied.
Risks and caveats: Reported concerns centre on DHA rather than on lotions in particular: contact dermatitis, a possible increase in free-radical formation in sun-exposed skin soon after application, and a lack of meaningful UV protection. Regulators approve DHA for external use and not for the eyes, lips or mucous membranes.
deepLead:
A gradual tanning lotion, also called a build-up tanner, is a lotion or moisturizer that contains a mild self-tanning agent so that colour deepens with repeated daily use. Encyclopedic sources say a slight change in skin colour is usually visible after the first application and darkens with more frequent use.
The most common active ingredient in sunless tanners is dihydroxyacetone (DHA), a three-carbon sugar that stains the outer skin layer through a browning (Maillard) reaction rather than by stimulating melanin. Drugstore self-tanners typically contain 3 to 5 percent DHA, with higher concentrations in professional products. Gradual lotions are generally formulated with less colour per application, though specific concentrations are not given in the sources reviewed.
No clinical studies of gradual tanning lotions as appearance products have been published in the sources reviewed. Safety discussion centres on DHA more broadly.

name: Tanning accelerator

angle.text: Users apply or take tanning accelerators hoping to darken faster during UV exposure. The melanin-boosting claim is untested, and users report skin effects such as acne and rashes.

summary: Topical or oral products, often tyrosine or psoralen-based, sold to speed up a UV tan; efficacy is unproven and users report more acne and rashes.
note: Used with UV exposure; a survey links use to frequent, high-risk indoor tanning and to skin reactions.
currentQuick:
Tanning accelerators are lotions (and sometimes pills) marketed to indoor and outdoor tanners to make a tan appear faster or darker. They typically contain the amino acid tyrosine, psoralens, or other chemicals, and are meant to be used together with UV exposure.
A 2015 survey of 200 indoor tanners found that just over half used them and that users tended to tan more often and to show more signs of tanning addiction. Encyclopedic sources say there is no scientific data supporting the claim that tyrosine boosts melanin formation in this way.
How it works: Marketing claims hold that tyrosine, a building block of melanin, increases pigment production when applied to the skin. Psoralens, such as 5-methoxypsoralen (bergapten), are photosensitizing compounds that sensitise skin to UV and have been used medically in psoriasis and vitiligo; they have also been described as sun-tanning accelerators.
Risks and caveats: In the 2015 survey, acne and rashes were more common among users, and adverse reactions stopped further use about 31 percent of the time. Psoralens are photosensitizers and a rhesus monkey study found a high share of topically applied 5-methoxypsoralen was absorbed. Accelerators are used with UV exposure, which is a documented cause of skin cancer.
deepLead:
Tanning accelerators are topical products, and sometimes pills, sold to speed up or deepen tanning when combined with UV exposure from sunlight or tanning beds. The ingredients described in the literature include tyrosine, psoralens and other chemicals. Wikipedia describes them as lotions or pills, usually containing tyrosine, that claim to boost melanin formation, and states that no scientific data currently supports these claims.
A 2015 survey in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology reported that 53 percent of 200 indoor tanners used accelerators, that users were more likely to spray tan, tan frequently and be addicted to tanning, and that acne and rashes were more common among them. The authors characterised users as high-risk indoor tanners.
No clinical trials of tyrosine or similar tanning accelerators for appearance have been found. The related compound 5-methoxypsoralen has been studied pharmacologically in animals and used medically for skin disease.

name: UPF clothing

chain: Fewer wrinkles and spots over time
angle.text: UPF clothing is worn as a no-reapplication way to limit sun exposure, which is promoted for keeping skin looking younger. The fabric's UV blocking is lab-rated; its effect on visible aging has not been studied directly.

summary: Fabric tested and labelled for how much UV it blocks, used as a no-reapplication alternative to sunscreen.
note: Protection depends on weave, colour, fit and wetness; wet or stretched fabric blocks less.
currentQuick:
UPF clothing is made from fabric tested for ultraviolet protection factor, a lab measure of how much sunburn-causing UV passes through the cloth. UPF 50+ is the top published category, rated as blocking at least about 98 percent of UV.
People who want to limit sun-related skin ageing, uneven pigmentation or skin cancer risk without applying sunscreen to covered areas use it, along with hats and shade. Evidence that clothing reduces UV reaching skin is strong in laboratory terms; direct trials of appearance outcomes are limited.
How it works: Fabric absorbs, reflects or scatters UV. Denser weave, darker colour, heavier weight and added UV absorbers raise the rating, while stretching, wetting and wear can lower it. Ratings are measured with instruments rather than by testing sunburn on people.
Risks and caveats: The clothing itself carries little risk. Documented limits are reduced protection when wet or stretched, heat retention in heavy dark fabrics, and uncovered skin remaining exposed. Standards in North America are industry-led test methods rather than a government approval.
deepLead:
UPF clothing, also called sun-protective clothing, is apparel made from fabrics rated for ultraviolet protection. The ultraviolet protection factor (UPF) is the ratio of sunburn-causing UV that passes through a fabric without it versus with it, similar in concept to sunscreen's SPF but measured with laboratory instruments rather than human sunburn testing.
Under the American ASTM classification, UPF 15 to 24 is rated good, 25 to 39 very good, and 40 to 50+ excellent, blocking roughly 93 to 98 percent or more of UV. Fabric factors that influence the rating include fibre content, weave, colour, finishing and additives, and the performance of a fabric changes with stretching, shrinkage, hydration, laundering and wear. A review from 1998 noted that an average-weight cotton T-shirt gives an SPF of about 7.
Sun-protective clothing is promoted for preventing sunburn, photoaging and skin cancer, and dermatology reviews list sun-protective clothing among recommended photoprotection measures including for skin of color. Randomized trials have tested clothing in children and behaviour programmes, but no trial reviewed measured appearance outcomes such as wrinkles or pigmentation.

name: Light box / SAD lamp

angle.text: Users run light boxes in winter to lift mood and keep sleep and energy steady, which they connect to looking more rested. The evidence is for seasonal depression; effects on appearance are untested.

summary: A bright-light lamp used for seasonal depression, with solid evidence for SAD and none yet for looks.
note: Evidence supports mood effects in seasonal affective disorder; appearance benefits are untested. People with mania tendency or eye or skin photosensitivity are advised to seek clinical advice.
currentQuick:
A light box, or SAD lamp, is a bright lamp that emits up to about 10,000 lux of filtered white light, far above ordinary indoor lighting. It is sitting-in-front-of-it therapy, usually used in the morning for seasonal affective disorder, a pattern of winter depression.
In looksmaxxing and fitness circles it comes up as a way to improve energy, mood, sleep timing and winter low spirits that people link to how they look and perform. A 2020 meta-analysis found bright light superior to placebo for SAD, but no study has tested light boxes for facial appearance.
How it works: Bright light is detected by light-sensitive retinal cells that suppress melatonin and help reset the body clock. Researchers also link seasonal depression to serotonin function and to a phase-delay of circadian rhythms, which morning light is thought to advance.
Risks and caveats: Reported side effects include headache, eye irritation, jumpiness and nausea, and light therapy can trigger mania in people prone to it. Sources list eye conditions sensitive to light, photosensitive skin conditions, porphyria and photosensitizing drugs or herbs as reasons for caution, and recommend clinician supervision.
deepLead:
A light box, commonly called a SAD lamp, is a device that gives off bright white light, typically up to 10,000 lux at a set distance, used for bright light therapy (BLT). It is the standard form of light therapy for seasonal affective disorder (SAD), a condition of recurrent winter depression that affects about 1 to 3 percent of adults in temperate climates and is more common in women.
A 2020 meta-analysis of 19 randomized trials found that bright light therapy of at least 1,000 lux was superior to dim-light or sham placebo for depression ratings and for treatment response in SAD, although the authors noted moderate heterogeneity and a moderate-to-high risk of bias. Light therapy has also been studied in non-seasonal depression, sleep problems in older adults, and agitation in dementia.
In appearance-focused communities, light boxes are occasionally mentioned as a mood or energy tool, and some users note that lamps sold online are weaker than clinic-grade units. No clinical studies have tested light boxes for appearance outcomes.

name: Mattress (medium-firm)

angle.text: People choose a medium-firm mattress for comfortable sleep and spinal support, which forums link to better posture and a more rested look. Sleep research links it to less back pain; facial or skeletal effects are untested.

summary: A middle-firmness mattress that sleep research links to less back pain, and that forums link to posture; nothing tests facial or skeletal looks.
note: Evidence is about back pain and sleep, not appearance; the main clinical mattress research is on pressure injuries in hospital patients.
currentQuick:
A medium-firm mattress balances support and cushioning so the spine stays roughly level. Sleep and back-pain research, including a 2003 randomized trial summarised by Wikipedia, has associated medium-firm beds with less chronic low back pain.
In looksmaxxing communities the interest is mainly posture and sleep quality, with some users reporting back pain from soft mattresses and some choosing very hard surfaces or the floor. No study has tested mattress firmness for facial structure, height or other appearance outcomes.
How it works: Firmness affects how much the body sinks and how the spine is aligned in lying positions. Wikipedia says firm mattresses are suggested for stomach sleepers and some back sleepers, soft ones for side sleepers, and medium ones for most back sleepers. Pressure-redistributing surfaces are also studied in hospitals to reduce pressure injuries.
Risks and caveats: A mattress carries little direct risk. Soft surfaces that sag under the lower back are blamed by forum users for back pain, and a very hard surface is not endorsed by the sources reviewed. Hospital research on pressure injuries uses specialised foam, air and alternating-pressure mattresses rather than medium-firm home beds.
deepLead:
A medium-firm mattress is a bed with an intermediate firmness rating, between soft and firm. Mattresses come in innerspring, foam (polyurethane, memory foam, latex), hybrid, air and water types, and no single numeric firmness scale is given in encyclopedic sources. A 2003 trial used the European Committee for Standardization's Hs scale.
Wikipedia reports that a 2003 randomized trial published in The Lancet linked medium-firm mattresses to less chronic low back pain and that a 2015 systematic review found medium-firm, custom-inflated mattresses best for pain and spinal alignment. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis has examined which mattress type should be chosen to avoid back pain and improve sleep quality.
Looksmaxxing forum users discuss mattress choice in relation to lower-back support and posture. No clinical studies have examined mattress firmness for appearance.

name: Home UVB booth

angle.text: Some users consider home UVB booths for tanning without much burning, drawing on their use for dermatology phototherapy. The device is established for skin conditions; cosmetic tanning use has not been studied.

summary: A stand-up narrowband UVB phototherapy cabinet meant for home skin treatment; it is a medical light device, and its use for cosmetic tanning has not been studied.
note: UV radiation is classed as a Group 1 carcinogen by the IARC; contraindications include photosensitising drugs and herbs.
currentQuick:
A home UVB booth is a full-body cabinet that emits narrowband ultraviolet-B light, typically around 311-313 nm. Dermatology uses this wavelength to treat conditions such as psoriasis, vitiligo and eczema, and some patients receive treatment at home instead of in a clinic.
In looksmaxxing and tanning circles the booth comes up as a way to darken skin using mostly UVB rather than the UVA-heavy light of salon sunbeds. Published research on these devices concerns skin disease, not cosmetic tanning, so there are no trials of a home UVB booth as a tanning tool.
How it works: Narrowband UVB acts on skin cells and the immune system in the treated areas, which is why it is used for inflammatory and pigment disorders. UVB also stimulates new melanin production over a few days, whereas UVA mainly darkens melanin already present. Salon sunbeds emit mostly UVA with a small UVB share, so a UVB-dominant booth differs from them in spectrum.
Risks and caveats: UV exposure is associated with progressive skin damage, skin cancer, cataracts and burns, and the IARC classifies UV radiation as a Group 1 carcinogen. Photosensitising drugs, some herbs (such as St John's wort), porphyria and photosensitive skin conditions are listed as contraindications to phototherapy. Medical use is normally supervised by a clinician, and rules on tanning devices vary by country.
deepLead:
A home UVB booth is a stand-up cabinet fitted with narrowband ultraviolet-B (NB-UVB) lamps, designed so that a person can receive whole-body phototherapy at home instead of attending a clinic. Narrowband UVB emits around 311-313 nanometres and is the most widely used form of phototherapy in dermatology . A large, high-power UVB booth can deliver full-body treatment at home as an alternative to office-based treatment .
The booth's established uses are medical. Phototherapy is used for psoriasis, atopic dermatitis, vitiligo and several other skin conditions . A randomised equivalence trial published in 2024 compared home-based and office-based NB-UVB for psoriasis . Researchers have not published trials of a home UVB booth as a cosmetic tanning device.
In appearance communities the booth appears as a tanning idea: because UVB triggers new melanin production while UVA mostly darkens existing pigment, some users see a UVB-rich unit as a different route to a tan from a salon sunbed . Public health bodies and researchers point out that UV radiation is a recognised carcinogen and that indoor tanning is associated with higher melanoma risk .

name: Concealer (for men)

chain: Dark circles and blemishes blend away
angle.text: Men use concealer to cover under-eye circles, blemishes and redness, and the evened-out tone is visible straight away. Looksmaxxing posters rate it a low-cost option, and male-specific research is limited.

summary: A pigmented cosmetic dabbed over dark circles, blemishes and redness to even out skin tone; a temporary cover rather than a treatment, with little male-specific research.
note: Covers the appearance of dark circles and blemishes while worn; it does not treat their cause.
currentQuick:
Concealer is a thick, highly pigmented makeup used on small areas, most often to mask under-eye dark circles, spots, redness and scars. It comes as liquid, cream, stick, pencil and cream-to-powder, and is blended in with fingers, a brush or a sponge.
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a quick, low-cost way to reduce the look of eye bags and uneven skin, and also as something some men feel self-conscious about buying or wearing. Research on concealer itself is sparse, and nearly all of it is not specific to men.
How it works: Concealer works optically: its pigment sits on top of the skin and blocks or neutralises the darker or redder tone beneath it. Makeup guides describe yellow or peach tones for dark circles, and green for redness such as pimples or rosacea, and recommend a shade one or two steps lighter than the skin for brightening [1].
Risks and caveats: Concealer is a cosmetic and is generally sold without prescription. Some products contain ingredients such as fragrance, mineral oil, dimethicone or talc [1]. A 2021 questionnaire study of 539 Korean adults examined links between cosmetic use and acne [4]. Because it only masks, it does not change the underlying cause of dark circles or blemishes.
deepLead:
Concealer is a cosmetic used to mask skin imperfections such as dark under-eye circles, blemishes and hyperpigmentation. It is similar to foundation but more heavily pigmented, usually applied in small amounts and then blended with a brush, sponge or fingertips . It can be worn over or under foundation, or on its own .
Products come in several forms: liquid, stick, cream, pencil and cream-to-powder, each with different coverage and finish . Colour theory is part of its use. Makeup references describe yellow-toned concealers for dark circles, green or blue tones to counteract red areas, and purple-tinted products for sallow complexions .
In looksmaxxing forums, concealer is described mostly in the context of under-eye bags and dark circles, and members discuss how to use it discreetly. Published research on concealer as a product is limited, and no study in the sources reviewed tests it in men specifically.

name: Eyebrow pencil / powder

angle.text: Pencils and powders fill gaps and define brow shape for a fuller look, visible as soon as applied. They are a daily-wear cosmetic used to frame the eyes.

summary: Pencils and powders that fill sparse or uneven brows with pigment; a daily-wear cosmetic with essentially no published research behind it.
note: Cosmetic cover only; it does not change hair growth.
currentQuick:
Eyebrow pencils and powders are makeup products used to outline, darken or fill in the brows. Pencils draw fine hair-like strokes, while powders (often applied with a small angled brush) give a softer, fuller finish.
In looksmaxxing and grooming discussions they are a way to change brow density or shape without surgery or transplants. Little published research exists on these products themselves, so what is known comes mainly from general descriptions of eyebrow cosmetics.
How it works: The products deposit pigment on the skin and hairs, filling gaps and sharpening the outline. Powders are usually matched closely to natural hair colour for a softer look [1]. They affect appearance only while worn and do not alter hair growth.
Risks and caveats: As ordinary cosmetics they carry the usual risk of skin irritation or allergy to ingredients in some individuals. The sources reviewed contain no studies on adverse effects specific to brow pencils or powders.
deepLead:
Eyebrow pencils and powders are cosmetics used to define the eyebrows or make them appear fuller, outlining the shape or filling sparse areas . Brow gels add texture so hairs look thicker, and brow powders or eyeshadows closely matched to natural hair colour suit people who want a softer, fuller look . Pencils in general, including concealer pencils, can also be used to define eyebrows .
Eyebrow shape has changed with fashion across history, from the removal and repainting of brows in 8th-century Japan to the thin plucked brows of the 1920s and 1930s . Wikipedia notes that more men in Western societies have begun plucking parts of their brows, although that claim is not cited . Other brow options include tattooing or microblading, transplants and surgical brow lifts .
No clinical studies of brow pencils or powders were found. The products are discussed in grooming guides rather than in the medical literature.

name: Hair styling clay & pomade

angle.text: Clay and pomade are used to shape and hold hair, giving matte texture or a slick shine that is visible immediately. They are styling aids for presentation, with no clinical research behind them.

summary: Wax-, oil- or clay-based products that hold and texture hair for a day; styling aids with no clinical research behind them.
note: Cosmetic hold only; heavy or oil-based products can take several washes to remove.
currentQuick:
Hair clay and pomade are styling products that shape and hold hair. Pomade is traditionally greasy, waxy or water-based and gives a shiny, slick finish; clay is a related category of styling paste.
They appear in grooming discussions as tools for styles such as the pompadour, quiff and textured crop. No clinical studies of them were found, and the evidence base is mostly product descriptions and history.
How it works: Pomades are mostly petroleum jelly, mineral oil or lanolin, often with beeswax for stiffness; water-based versions use polymers and hardening agents. Wax-type products stay pliable and hold hair in place without drying out like alcohol-heavy gels do [1][2][3].
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia reports that some styling-product ingredients can strip oils or build up on hair, contributing to dryness, and that petroleum-based pomades can take several washes to remove; claims about follicle clogging or hair loss rest on non-clinical sources [1][3]. A 2023 measurement study of Beijing hair salons found that styling products including clay, wax and gel release volatile organic compounds [4].
deepLead:
Hair clay and pomade are styling products used to shape and hold hair. Pomade is a greasy, waxy or water-based product that gives a shiny, slick appearance, holds longer than most hair products and often takes repeated washes to remove . Clay is a related category of styling product; general encyclopedic coverage of it is thin .
Traditional pomades were made from bear fat or lard in the 18th and 19th centuries, with petroleum jelly, beeswax and lard more common by the early 1900s . Modern oil-based pomades typically contain lanolin, beeswax and petroleum jelly in heavy, medium or light holds, while water-based pomades use polymers and are easier to wash out . The products are central to pompadour, quiff, ducktail and undercut styles .
No clinical studies of hair clay or pomade were found. The best available data concern emissions: a 2023 study sampled products in Beijing salons and measured their volatile organic compound output .

name: Cologne / perfume

angle.text: Users wear cologne for a pleasant scent and a stronger impression in person. It is popular in grooming circles, and published trials of its effect on attractiveness were not found.

summary: Alcohol-based fragrance worn for scent and impression; popular in grooming circles, with no published trials of its effect on attractiveness in the sources reviewed.
note: Fragrance ingredients are a known cause of contact allergy and skin irritation in some people.
currentQuick:
Perfume is a blend of aroma compounds, fixatives and a solvent, usually ethanol, worn on skin or clothing. 'Cologne' originally meant the citrus-based eau de Cologne first sold in Cologne, Germany in 1709, and in American English it now usually means a men's fragrance.
On looksmaxxing forums fragrance is treated as a low-effort add-on to grooming, with members ranking popular bottles and debating whether scent matters if the face does not. No study in the sources reviewed tests whether wearing cologne changes perceived attractiveness.
How it works: Fragrances evaporate in stages, with top notes disappearing first and base notes lasting longest. The strength of the formulation changes how long it lasts: Wikipedia lists parfum at about 15-30% aromatic compounds, eau de parfum at 15-20%, eau de toilette at 5-15% and eau de cologne at 2-3%, with brands varying [2]. The scent is smelled by others; any effect on social impressions is not established by trial data.
Risks and caveats: Fragrance ingredients can cause contact dermatitis, headaches or asthma symptoms in sensitive people, and patch testing with fragrance mix gives a positive reaction in about 10% of people with eczema, according to Wikipedia [3]. A 2020 review of essential oils, which are common in fragrance, also describes adverse effects including endocrine-disrupting properties for some oils [5].
deepLead:
Perfume is a mixture of fragrant essential oils or aroma compounds, fixatives and solvents, usually in liquid form. Fine fragrance typically uses ethanol or an ethanol-water mix as the solvent . Products are classed by concentration, from parfum or extrait at about 15-30% down through eau de parfum, eau de toilette and eau de cologne at about 2-3%, though the terms are imprecise and brands differ .
Eau de Cologne ('water from Cologne') began as a citrus-based fragrance launched in Cologne, Germany in 1709 by the Italian perfumer Giovanni Maria Farina; the name later became a generic term for lightly concentrated scented waters of about 2-5% concentration . In American English, 'cologne' usually refers to a men's fragrance, even when the product is an eau de toilette or eau de parfum .
Looksmaxxing forums place fragrance among grooming and 'style' tools. A looksmax.org thread ranks popular men's bottles by price and states that colognes 'only work' if a person is already good-looking . No study in the sources reviewed tests whether wearing cologne improves perceived attractiveness, and published research relevant to fragrance concerns allergy and the health effects of ingredients .

name: Rhinoplasty

angle.text: Rhinoplasty is discussed as the main facial-harmony operation, used to change the nose's shape and size, and the result is visibly and measurably different after healing. The idea that nose changes shift the whole face is based on opinion.

summary: Surgery that reshapes the nose for looks or breathing; the most discussed facial 'harmony' operation in looksmaxxing, with real revision and complication rates.
note: Swelling can take a year to settle, and revision surgery is needed in roughly 5-20% of cases according to published figures.
currentQuick:
Rhinoplasty is plastic surgery that changes the shape, size or proportions of the nose, or improves breathing. It is done for cosmetic reasons, for functional ones such as an obstructed airway, and for reconstruction after injury, birth defects or cancer. Surgery limited to the septum is called septoplasty.
In looksmaxxing communities the nose is treated as a central feature of facial harmony, and rhinoplasty is frequently discussed alongside jaw surgery and fillers. Published sources describe it as a long-established operation, with high reported satisfaction in several studies but also a meaningful revision rate and a need for psychological screening before cosmetic surgery.
How it works: Surgeons reshape the nasal bones and cartilages, adding, removing or repositioning tissue, and sometimes grafting cartilage from the septum, ear or rib. Access is either through incisions inside the nose (closed) or with an added incision across the columella (open). Preservation techniques try to keep the existing dorsum rather than cutting it down [1][4].
Risks and caveats: Reported complications include breathing impairment, asymmetry, collapse of tip support and prolonged swelling that can take up to a year to resolve; smoking impairs healing [1]. Secondary (revision) surgery is needed in roughly 5-20% of operations, and revisions are technically harder [1]. Body dysmorphic disorder is more common among cosmetic surgery patients and is associated with dissatisfaction, which is why screening is recommended [3][8].
deepLead:
Rhinoplasty, informally a 'nose job', is plastic surgery that changes the shape, size or proportions of the nose or improves its function. It takes two broad forms: reconstructive surgery, which restores form and function after injury, birth defects or failed earlier surgery, and cosmetic surgery, which changes appearance . Surgery limited to the septum is called septoplasty .
The operation has an unusually long history, with nasal repair described in the Edwin Smith Papyrus and in the Sushruta Samhita of ancient India, and a modern endonasal technique reported by John Orlando Roe in 1887 . Common cosmetic goals include reducing a dorsal hump, narrowing the nostrils or tip, and changing the nasolabial angle . Techniques now include open and closed approaches, cartilage grafting, ultrasonic (piezoelectric) bone cutting, and dorsal preservation .
Within looksmaxxing forums, rhinoplasty is among the most discussed surgeries, often described as a change in 'facial harmony' and compared against jaw surgery and fillers. Published sources report that revision surgery is needed in roughly 5-20% of cases and that swelling can last up to a year . Researchers recommend screening cosmetic surgery candidates for body dysmorphic disorder .

name: Bimaxillary osteotomy (bimax)

angle.text: Bimax repositions both jaws and is sought for bite and airway problems as well as for changing facial proportions, with visible skeletal change after healing. The structural operation is established; the cosmetic results forums describe vary by case.

summary: Double-jaw surgery that repositions both upper and lower jaw; an established operation for bite and airway problems that forums also treat as the big facial-structure move.
note: Major surgery under general anaesthesia with a long recovery; nerve numbness, relapse and joint problems are documented.
currentQuick:
Bimaxillary osteotomy, usually shortened to bimax, is an operation in which a surgeon cuts both the upper jaw (maxilla) and lower jaw (mandible) through the mouth, moves them to a new position and fixes them with plates and screws. In clinical practice it is used for bite problems such as underbites and overbites, for jaw-joint problems and for obstructive sleep apnoea.
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as the surgical route to a more forward, balanced facial skeleton, often with a counter-clockwise rotation of the jaws. Published research supports it for bite and airway outcomes and reports high patient satisfaction with appearance, but formal evidence on purely cosmetic results is limited.
How it works: Bone cuts allow the maxilla (typically with a Le Fort I osteotomy) and the mandible (typically with a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy) to be moved forward, back, up, down or rotated. Orthodontic braces usually align the teeth before and after surgery, and 3D virtual planning is increasingly used to plan the movements.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection, temporary or permanent numbness of the lip and chin, temporomandibular joint problems, condylar resorption, relapse of the jaw position and the need for months of recovery and orthodontics. It is performed under general anaesthesia and is regulated as ordinary surgery in most countries; cosmetic-only indications are judged case by case by surgeons.
deepLead:
Bimaxillary osteotomy, commonly called bimax or double-jaw surgery, is a form of orthognathic (corrective jaw) surgery in which both the upper jaw and the lower jaw are cut, repositioned and fixed in a new position, usually through incisions inside the mouth. It is used for bite discrepancies, jaw-joint problems, facial asymmetry and obstructive sleep apnoea, and is also sought by people who want to change facial proportions.
Systematic reviews and trials around the procedure mostly examine planning methods, anaesthesia, pain control and blood loss rather than cosmetic outcomes. One review of bimaxillary osteotomy for sleep apnoea reports sustained improvements in breathing measures and reports that many patients also describe a positive change in facial aesthetics. Reported disadvantages include temporary or permanent sensory disturbance and a temporary restriction of jaw function.
On forums such as looksmax.org the procedure is discussed alongside Le Fort I advancement, genioplasty, braces, implants and rhinoplasty as part of a larger facial-surgery plan, with frequent questions about insurance coverage, orthodontic preparation and surgery abroad.

name: LeFort 1 maxillary advancement

angle.text: LeFort 1 advances the upper jaw and is discussed for adding midface projection, with the bone movement visible and measurable. The operation is standard for bite problems; claims of under-eye support rest mostly on bite and cleft research.

summary: Upper-jaw surgery that cuts and moves the maxilla forward for midface projection; a standard orthognathic operation whose cosmetic claims rest mostly on bite and cleft research.
note: Major surgery under general anaesthesia; relapse, numbness and bite or joint problems are documented, and stability varies with the direction of movement.
currentQuick:
A Le Fort I osteotomy is a horizontal cut through the upper jaw, made from inside the mouth, that lets the surgeon move the maxilla forward, back, up or down and fix it with plates. In clinical practice it is used for bite problems, a recessed or vertically long upper jaw, cleft-related underdevelopment and, together with lower-jaw surgery, for sleep apnoea.
Looksmaxxing forums discuss it as a way to project the midface, support the area under the eyes and correct underbites, often paired with a lower-jaw operation. Published studies document stability and outcomes in functional and cleft patients; there is little research on cosmetic-only advancement.
How it works: The bone cut passes above the tooth roots and below the cheekbone and eye socket, freeing the tooth-bearing maxilla so it can be repositioned in three dimensions. Plates and screws hold the new position while bone heals; orthodontics aligns the teeth around the operation.
Risks and caveats: Documented concerns include bleeding, swelling, infection, nerve numbness, relapse of the new position (greater for some movement directions and large advancements), nasal and lip changes and a months-long recovery. It is regulated as routine surgery and performed by oral and maxillofacial or craniofacial surgeons.
deepLead:
Le Fort I osteotomy is an upper-jaw operation in which the maxilla is cut horizontally above the roots of the teeth, mobilised and fixed in a new position, usually through an incision inside the mouth. It is the most common maxillary procedure in orthognathic surgery and can advance, set back, shorten, lengthen or expand the upper jaw. In looksmaxxing circles it is known as LeFort 1 or maxilla advancement and is discussed as a method of increasing midface projection.
Clinical research on the operation comes mainly from bite-correction and cleft lip and palate patients. Reviews and studies report that its stability depends on the direction of movement, the fixation method and the technique, and that cleft patients often need maxillary advancement because earlier repair surgery can restrict maxillary growth. Studies of purely cosmetic advancement are limited.
Forum discussions on looksmax.org describe advancement distances of several millimetres, counter-clockwise rotation, effects on lip seal and under-eye support, and combination with lower-jaw surgery; these are reported experiences rather than trial findings.
